questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a declared column type commits you to
questions.learningObjective: State what declaring a column numeric commits the data to
questions.stem: In a clerk's file note, a column is declared numeric; what does that declaration commit the dataset to?

options.text: The column must store numeric values and support numeric operations
The column only changes how values are displayed on screen
options.misconception: treats a type declaration as a display format only

options.text: The column must be indexed for faster searching
options.misconception: confuses type declaration with index creation

options.text: The column can hold any text without validation
options.misconception: assumes declared types impose no constraints

questions.explanation: Declaring a column numeric fixes its domain to numbers and enables arithmetic. It is not merely cosmetic, and it does not by itself create an index.
questions.hint: A declared type restricts what values fit.

options.text: Rescale it to the zero to one range

questions.topic: A duplicate row and a duplicate key
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish duplicate key from duplicate row
questions.stem: Clerk note: a case key repeats with different dates; is that a duplicate row?

answer.exemplar: No, it is a duplicate key rather than a duplicate row, because the key repeats but other fields differ; the records may represent separate events.

questions.explanation: A duplicate key repeats an identifier while other attributes differ. It is not an exact duplicate row and may need merging or event handling.
questions.hint: Compare all columns, not just the key.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: An outlier and a valid extreme
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether to keep an extreme
questions.stem: Clerk note: one value of 200 appears among 99 values averaging 50; what is the mean of all 100?
questions.explanation: The 99 sum to 4950, plus 200 gives 5150, divided by 100 is 51.5. The extreme raises the mean only modestly.
questions.hint: Sum the 99 then add the extreme.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why distance-based methods need a common scale
questions.learningObjective: State why scaling matters for distance
questions.stem: Clerk note: why is standardisation needed before computing distances?

options.text: To speed up file loading
To delete low-variance features
To convert categories to numbers
To make all features equally influential

questions.explanation: Standardisation gives each feature comparable influence on distance. It does not select features or encode categories.
questions.hint: Equal influence is the goal.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why gradient methods need a common scale
questions.learningObjective: State why scaling matters for gradients
questions.stem: Clerk note: what does scaling do for gradient descent?

options.text: It increases the number of features
It removes outliers automatically
It makes the loss surface better conditioned
It guarantees convergence in one step

questions.explanation: Scaling improves the conditioning of the loss surface, allowing a single learning rate to make steady progress.
questions.hint: Conditioning improves learning.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The ordinal imputation trap
questions.learningObjective: Explain the ordinal trap
questions.stem: Clerk note: why is a fractional mean fill risky for an ordinal rating?

options.text: It requires dropping the column
It always lowers the variance
options.misconception: focuses on variance rather than validity

options.text: It makes the data categorical
It creates a category that does not exist

questions.explanation: A fractional mean fill invents a rating level that was never observed. Use a median or mode level instead.
questions.hint: The fill must be an observed level.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Counting cells after a clean
questions.learningObjective: Compute total cells
questions.stem: Clerk note: a 15 by 6 table has 12 missing cells; how many non-missing cells remain?
questions.explanation: Fifteen rows times six columns is 90 cells; subtracting 12 missing leaves 78 non-missing cells.
questions.hint: Multiply then subtract missing.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The mean of a rating column
questions.learningObjective: Compute a mean rating
questions.stem: Clerk note: ratings are 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5; what is the mean?
questions.explanation: The sum is 20 across 6 ratings, so the mean is 3.33. This summarises the observed ratings.
questions.hint: Sum the ratings and divide by six.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A blank that means zero
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish structural zero from missing
questions.stem: Clerk note: a discount field is blank for ineligible clients; is it missing?

answer.exemplar: No, the blank means no discount applies, so it should be zero; treating it as missing would invent discounts.

questions.explanation: A blank that structurally means zero is not missing data. Imputing it would fabricate a discount.
questions.hint: Ineligibility means zero discount.

questions.topic: Turning a missing percentage into a count
questions.learningObjective: Convert percent missing to count
questions.stem: Clerk note: 15 percent of 200 files lack a signature; how many are missing?
questions.explanation: Fifteen percent of 200 is 30 files, so 30 signatures are missing.
questions.hint: Multiply 200 by 0.15.

questions.topic: The value mean imputation writes
questions.learningObjective: Compute a mean fill
questions.stem: Clerk note: observed values are 5, 9, 13, 17; what does mean imputation write?
questions.explanation: The mean of 5, 9, 13, 17 is 11.0, which fills each missing cell.
questions.hint: Sum then divide by four.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How far the median fill sits below the mean
questions.learningObjective: Compute mean minus median
questions.stem: Clerk note: mean value is 80 and median value is 74; how far below the mean is the median?
questions.explanation: The median sits 6 units below the mean, showing right skew. Median imputation is preferred when extremes pull the mean up.
questions.hint: Subtract median from mean.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The share a mode fill creates
questions.learningObjective: Compute the post-fill share of the mode
questions.stem: Clerk note: a category appears 18 times and 6 values are missing; what share of 24 would the mode fill create?
questions.explanation: After filling, the mode category occupies all 24 of 24 rows, a share of 1.0. That concentration is the cost of mode imputation.
questions.hint: Divide filled total by all rows.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The cost of a blanket drop
questions.learningObjective: Compute remaining rows after a drop
questions.stem: Clerk note: a blanket drop removes 18 of 90 rows; how many rows remain?
questions.explanation: Removing 18 rows leaves 72 rows for analysis. That loss must be weighed against the benefit of complete cases.
questions.hint: Subtract 18 from 90.
